source.title: Boosting Cross-lingual Transferability in Multilingual Models via In-Context Learning
source.authors: SunKyoung Kim; Dayeon Ki; Yireun Kim; Jinsik Lee

record.file_problem: The full paper text is present; no apparent truncation or garbling.
record.tranche_reason: It tests whether downstream task performance changes with model scale, using cross-lingual XQuAD F1 rather than held-out pretraining loss.
record.gate_note: The paper reports a model-scale comparison for average XQuAD F1 and explicitly states the 1B-to-7B performance gains for Cross-lingual QA prompting. It does not test pretraining loss, parameter/token/compute power laws, extrapolation from small training runs, or compute-optimal allocations. Figure 2 also plots other prompting methods, but the plot's individual point values are not unambiguously assignable from the supplied text.
record.test_reason: A prompting-method paper with a side analysis (Figure 2) of downstream XQuAD F1 across three sizes of XGLM and BLOOM. This gives a weak, new-setting result on V6: multilingual cross-lingual in-context QA. There are only three sizes, no fitted trend, and no pretraining loss.
record.authors_conclusion: Partly right but incomplete. The main conclusion is that Cross-lingual QA prompting, which translates only the question-answer pairs, elicits cross-lingual knowledge and matches or beats monolingual prompting. As a secondary claim, the authors say larger models narrow the gap between Target Language and Cross-lingual QA prompting, and that gains with size follow 'the scaling law (Kaplan et al., 2020)'.
record.recipe_differences: This is a downstream cross-lingual task-performance comparison across model-size variants, not a fit of held-out pretraining loss against parameters, tokens, or compute.
record.method_sensitivity: The scale result is reported for Cross-lingual QA prompting; Figure 2 also displays source- and target-language prompting, but the supplied text does not give unambiguous numerical point values for those curves.
record.peer_reviewed: Proceedings of the 1st Workshop on In-Context Learning at the 41st International Conference on Machine Learning (2024)
record.problems: The scale comparison covers only XQuAD, two model families, and a small number of model sizes. The paper does not report uncertainty for the scale gains in the supplied text, and does not measure pretraining loss or training compute.
record.rows_left_out: Figure 2 plots source- and target-language prompting series as well, but individual point values could not be assigned confidently from the supplied text; no numerical rows were created for those plotted points.

untested.parts: Whether gains follow a predictable functional form, such as a power law or a fit that extrapolates. Downstream performance as a function of pretraining loss. Scale beyond 7B. Scale effects on XNLI, XCOPA and MLQA, which are reported only at 7B.
Not tested: no pretraining loss measured.

missing.what: Source- and Target-Language prompting XQuAD F1 across sizes; all three methods also rise with size. The 7B endpoints are readable from Table 3: XGLM 35.19 and 38.08, BLOOM 34.56 and 36.41.

record.verdict_notes: This is a weak test of V6. The authors invoke Kaplan et al. loosely to describe a three-point monotonic increase; no scaling law is fitted. No uncertainty is reported for the scale gains. Figure 2 values in the extracted text are garbled and only partly assignable. XGLM and BLOOM differ in training data, so the two size ladders are not comparable with each other.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out pretraining loss as a function of parameters, tokens, or compute.
Prediction of much larger-run pretraining loss from smaller-run fits.
Loss-minimising parameter and token allocations at fixed compute.
Effects of depth, width, and other architecture details at fixed parameter count.
Power-law behavior beyond standard text pretraining.
The study tests downstream performance versus model scale on XQuAD under Cross-lingual QA prompting; it does not test downstream performance versus pretraining loss or other tasks and settings.
Dependence of fitted scaling exponents or compute-optimal allocations on setup and fitting choices.

rows.subject: XGLM
rows.size_stated: 1.7B, 2.9B, and 7.5B variants; the reported gain is for 1B to 7B scale labels in Figure 2
rows.operation_detail: Compared average XQuAD performance across model-size variants using Cross-lingual QA prompting.
rows.baseline: 1B-scale performance (Figure 2; numerical value not stated in text)
rows.locator: Section 5, Model Performance at Scale; Figure 2
rows.note: The paper states that average performance increases consistently from 1B to 7B and reports this gain for XGLM.
rows.check: Smallest XGLM variant is 1.7B, not 1B; the '1B' is Figure 2's approximate axis label. Subject, value and state are otherwise fine. The row measures the authors' own prompting method across scale; it is kept because it is a downstream-vs-scale measurement.

rows.subject: BLOOM
rows.operation_detail: Compared average XQuAD performance across model-size variants using Cross-lingual QA prompting.
rows.baseline: 1B-scale performance (Figure 2; numerical value not stated in text)
rows.locator: Section 5, Model Performance at Scale; Figure 2
rows.note: The paper states that average performance increases consistently from 1B to 7B and reports this gain for BLOOM.
rows.check: No substantive error. Gain of +7.25 is from the text; Figure 2 point values are only approximately readable (7B CLQA 37.2, matching Table 3's 37.22).

relationships.condition: XGLM (1.7B–7.5B) and BLOOM (1B–7B), Cross-lingual QA 5-shot prompting, average XQuAD F1
relationships.reason: F1 rises consistently from smallest to 7B: +4.27 for XGLM (r1) and +7.25 for BLOOM (r2). This is only three sizes per family with no fit, so it shows monotonic improvement rather than predictability.
relationships.display_finding: XQuAD F1 increased consistently by 4.27 for XGLM and 7.25 for BLOOM across three sizes per family, without a predictive fit.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
